props.title: Zero Hour!

sections.content: **Zero Hour!** (1957) stands as the unintentional blueprint for **Airplane!** (1980), so much so that the later comedy purchased the rights to remake it almost shot-for-shot. This tense disaster thriller follows Ted Stryker, a former WWII pilot with PTSD, who must land a commercial airplane when the crew and passengers fall ill from food poisoning. The film established many disaster movie tropes that would later define the 1970s genre explosion, directly influencing Airport (1970) and its numerous sequels. Director Hall Bartlett crafts genuine suspense through claustrophobic cockpit scenes and Sterling Hayden's commanding performance as the ground control expert.

movies.slug: John Wayne stars as a veteran pilot helping land a troubled plane over the Pacific. Set the template for airborne disaster films.

sections.content: The late 1950s saw a fascinating surge in aviation-themed disaster films, reflecting both post-war anxiety and the boom in commercial air travel. **The Crowded Sky** (1960) and **Fate Is the Hunter** (1964) followed similar templates, but **Zero Hour!** (1957) stands out for its lean efficiency and lack of melodramatic subplots. The film's influence extends beyond disaster movies - its documentary-style approach to technical procedures influenced films like **United 93** (2006) and Sully (2016).

What makes **Zero Hour!** (1957) particularly notable is its handling of PTSD, rare for its era. Ted Stryker's trauma isn't just a plot device but a central character element that adds psychological depth. This approach would later be echoed in films like **The Right Stuff** (1983) and **Flight** (2012), where pilot psychology plays a crucial role in the narrative. SUBHEAD: Legacy and Impact on Aviation Films

movies.title: Sully
movies.slug: Tom Hanks portrays Captain Chesley Sullenberger in the true story of the Miracle on the Hudson landing.

sections.content: The film's DNA is evident in countless aviation thrillers, from **Executive Decision** (1996) to **Non-Stop** (2014). Its greatest legacy, however, might be as the inspiration for **Airplane!** (1980), which copied entire scenes and dialogue verbatim for comedic effect. The serious delivery of lines that would later become iconic jokes ("Joey, have you ever been in a Turkish prison?") demonstrates how thin the line between tension and absurdity can be in the disaster genre.
